episode: The next big breakthrough will be AIs learning on the job
what: Explores the paradigm shift in AI where models learn continuously in real-world environments, not just during training. Discusses RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verification and Refinement), learning generalization, and implications for 2027.
why: This is a foundational shift in AI deployment and training, with direct implications for product development, model efficiency, and long-term autonomy.

Dwarkesh Patel Jun 26, 2026 118 31 8 Share Transcript Here’s the big research bet the labs are making currently : if we train AIs to accomplish millions of verifiable tasks across thousands of diverse RL environments, then we’ll basically have built AGI. Because such training will create these general problem solving skills (like how to make progress on an open ended task for weeks on end in the face of errors, mistakes, and ambiguity). The people optimistic about this vision would say that anything we might consider a fundamental deficits with the current learning paradigm—for example, data inefficiency and lack of continual learning—can be steamrolled by just scaling training more, just as all the supposed “fundamental” research problems in natural language processing collapsed against the flood of compute thrown into LLMs. Yes, these models are 1/1-millionth as sample efficient as humans during training. But training a one-time cost amortized across billions of user sessions. What matters is how smart, general, and sample efficient the model is within a session , and that’s clearly been improving as we do more RL training. AIs are able to solve more and more ambitious problems across longer and longer time spans - anybody who’s been using these models for coding knows that. Similarly, continual learning—as defined as the model’s weights getting updated from deployment—may simply not be necessary. Again, because if in-context learning gets so good across longer and longer horizons, then we don’t need to distill back to weights to get on-the-job learning. People often say that their employees are not net productive until six months or more on the job, so clearly online learning is necessary for competence. But what if you could just fit those six months into the context window? There’s been tons of architectural innovations on the transformer which dramatically increase the length of context you can store. With a couple more years of progress, why couldn’t we have arbitrarily large context windows? Grindability is just as important as verifiability To address whether this will work, I want to first take a detour and ask a question about the current nature of AI progress that I find confusing and interesting. Why has progress on computer use been so slow? Computer use is so clearly verifiable (did the desired Etsy item get ordered, is everything I need corporate for my event booked, have my taxes been submitted). So isn’t it weird that computer use has been making much slower progress than coding and math and other verifiable domains? There’s many reasons for this, I’m sure, among them the fact that the models are exposed to far less high quality multimodal data during pretraining, and that video consumes the context window far faster. [1] But one reason that I think it quite underrated, and also which reveals the canyon walls against which the river of AI progress will only slowly chip away at, is that it is not enough for a domain to be verifiable. It also has to be very grindable—in the sense that you can run lots of parallel rollouts against a deterministic and replayable simulator. If you’re trying to make a model better at coding, you can create an environment that has a software repo with some missing feature that you’ve tasked the AIs with creating, and then you have a thousand parallel agents just go at the problem, each with their identical copy of the container. [2] But this doesn’t work with computer use—at least not trivially. You can’t have a thousand agents go try the same checkout flow on Amazon.com. Because Andy Jassy will find and detect your bots and shut your ass down. You can solve this by making clones of Slack, Gmail, and all the other common applications and websites. But at least currently, this is a very labor-intensive and unscalable way to build environments. Of course, once AIs get good enough at coding to themselves build these clones with extremely high fidelity, then I’m sure computer use will make a ton of progress. And you’re also killing two birds with one stone with this kind of procedure, because getting AIs to rebuild whole complex applications from scratch is a great RL objective for coding as well. But while computer use itself may soon be solved, its current lethargy tells us the following: that unless you can build a very replayable training target for a domain, the models will struggle to make much progress. The reason this is true is, of course, that the models are incredibly sample inefficient during training. This is the point I was making in my last monologue . In computer use, we might be able to make up for this sample efficiency deficit by building these farmable deterministic simulators. But for so many different other kinds of skills an AGI would need to learn, we simply can’t do this. How would we train an AI to build a business? How would you make an AI that’s really good at winning court cases? Or having a profitable day trading in the markets? Or helping a candidate win an election? The rollout requires interacting with the world and cannot be recreated simply within the datacenter. And the outer loop verification may take months or years of real world actions to elicit, and cannot be re-observed by perturbing the model’s actions thousands of times in parallel so that you can isolate what exactly the model did that actually worked. Dealing with such reset-free non-stationary environments is a known open problem in RL. I’m not pointing out anything new. But I really do want to emphasize that because of the idiosyncratic and sparse nature of the data in most domains in the world, you need sample efficiency in order to get proficient. If AIs are to develop all the skills that humans have, and even skills that no humans have, then they need to be able to learn from information revealed in unstructured, unverifiable, and ambiguous ways from scarce amounts of real world interaction. Because in many domains, the relevant training information simply doesn’t exist in any other way. What is the RL environment to make an AI as good at politics as Lyndon Johnson, or as good at building a space launch business as Elon Musk? Will RLVR alone generalize? The labs are betting that RLVR will generalize to all these other domains. episode: AI Is Crossing the Frontier of Human Knowledge | Kevin Weil
what: Kevin Weil (former VP of Science at OpenAI) discusses AI's role in accelerating scientific discovery, from math to medicine. Highlights AI agents, robotic labs, and new startup opportunities.
why: Direct insight from a former OpenAI exec on how AI is being applied to frontier science and product design.
audio_transcript_notes:
### Chunk 1
- **[Kevin Weil]**: AI is now solving problems that humans have never solved before, going beyond the frontier of human knowledge.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: AGI will change lives not just by automating tasks, but by directly contributing to scientific discovery.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Goal: Accelerate science—bring the breakthroughs of 2050 into 2030.  
- **[Speaker]**: Most people see AI as a productivity tool, but Weil believes its biggest impact may be in expanding humanity’s capacity for discovery.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Previously CPO and VP of Science at OpenAI; focused on AI’s role in scientific breakthroughs, not just code or content generation.  
- **[Speaker]**: AI can accelerate progress in mathematics, medicine, material science, and other foundational fields.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: GPT-5 and Gemini models have solved ~10–12 open mathematics problems in January alone—problems humans hadn’t yet solved.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Models are not yet solving problems that humans *couldn’t* solve, but they are going beyond what humans *had* solved.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: AI’s progression in capability is rapid: from “can’t do” → “barely can do” → “great at it” in 6–12 months.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Frontier science is in the “glimmer” phase with AI—showing early signs of novel problem-solving.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: The most tangible impact of AGI may be in scientific domains: new materials, superconductivity, personalized medicine, understanding the universe.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Codex and AI coding tools have already expanded programming access by orders of magnitude, unleashing creativity.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Example: a small city official had data and ideas but no way to implement solutions—Codex could now do it via prompts.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Recently launched *Prism*—an AI-native environment for scientific writing and collaboration.  
- **[Kevin Weil]**: Personal anecdote: Feels time wasted if not using AI agents (e.g., Codex) during meetings or overnight.  
- **[Speaker]**: AI is shifting from augmentation to autonomous execution of complex tasks.  
- **[DJ takeaway]**: AI is now a discovery engine, not just a productivity tool—implications for science, policy, and long-term economic growth.  
- **[DJ takeaway]**: Track AI breakthroughs in math and science as leading indicators of AGI progress.  
- **[DJ takeaway]**: Codex and similar tools are already enabling non-experts to implement ideas—democratizing innovation.  
- **[DJ takeaway]**: AI-native tools like *Prism* signal a new category of scientific infrastructure.  
- **[DJ counterpoint]**: Skepticism remains about whether AI is truly doing novel thinking or synthesizing known knowledge.  
- **[DJ framework]**: Use the “zero → 5–10% → 60–80%” model to assess AI capabilities in any domain.

### Chunk 2
- **Creativity unleashed via AI parallels historical disruptions (e.g., furniture-making)**:  
  - Like the industrial revolution in furniture, AI enables mass production of creative output previously limited to individual craftsmanship.  
  - This leads to disorientation due to the speed and scale of disruption.  
  - However, it also democratizes access to high-quality output (e.g., websites, content), enabling broader use by many more people.

- **Bespoke vs. mass-produced tension remains**:  
  - Despite AI-driven automation, there's still value in human-made, custom work (e.g., custom furniture, bespoke websites).  
  - This mirrors how some people still drive manually despite autonomous vehicles—niche but valued.

- **High agency individuals are selected for in this AI era**:  
  - High agency, curiosity, and fast learning are now more valuable than ever.  
  - Tools like Codex allow people to parallelize idea generation and implementation—e.g., start a task in the morning and have it implemented by evening while doing other work.

- **OpenAI’s vision for AI in science**:  
  - Focus on math, physics, theoretical CS because they are in silico-friendly and allow closed-loop optimization.  
  - Goal: teach models to think for extended periods (days/weeks) to solve harder problems—going beyond short-term reasoning.  
  - Long-term aim: accelerate real-world scientific progress (e.g., medicine, materials science) through AI-driven discovery.

- **Limitations of in silico approaches**:  
  - Real-world experimentation still required—e.g., drug discovery, biology.  
  - Simulations will increase in importance but must be validated through physical experiments.

- **Future of science involves robotic labs and reinforcement learning loops**:  
  - AI models will design experiments, simulate, refine, and send to robotic labs for execution.  
  - Results feed back into the model, creating a continuous loop.  
  - Robotic labs can scale horizontally and operate 24/7, accelerating the pace of experimentation beyond human limitations.

- **Grad students will shift to higher-level, human-centric tasks**:  
  - As robotic labs handle repetitive tasks (e.g., pipetting), human researchers will focus on creative and strategic aspects of science.

- **Timeline and prerequisites for this future**:  
  - Some components (e.g., robotic labs, AI solving math problems) already exist and in early adopter phase.  
  - Key enablers: robotics, scalable infrastructure, and tighter integration between simulation and real-world experimentation.  
  - Given current momentum, this future is not far off.

- **Product decisions at scale are often controversial but data-driven**:  
  - Example: Twitter feed ranking—initially seen as a betrayal of Twitter’s real-time ethos.  
  - Despite backlash, data showed strong positive engagement metrics (e.g., double-digit increases).  
  - Similar pattern seen with Facebook’s original newsfeed rollout.

- **UX challenges with reasoning models (e.g., GPT-4o)**:  
  - Unlike chat models, reasoning models take time to process.  
  - Design challenge: how to communicate ongoing thought without exposing full chain-of-thought (due to IP/geopolitical concerns).  
  - UX considerations: should users wait, come back later, or watch a curated progress indicator?

### Chunk 3
- **User experience (UX) design for AI should mirror human behavior**:  
  - If a human can immediately answer a question (like GPT-4 style), they respond instantly.  
  - If the question requires thought, humans don’t just “babble” or go silent; they provide periodic updates.  
  - AI models are being designed to mimic this behavior—giving “cliffs notes” of their thinking before delivering a final answer.

- **Product development tension: data vs. taste**:  
  - There’s a recurring debate between relying on data and trusting intuition (or “taste”).  
  - Blindly following data can lead to passive decision-making; taste can guide vision before data catches up.  
  - Anecdotes (user feedback) are often valuable and shouldn’t be dismissed—can indicate bimodal user behavior masked by averages.

- **Interpreting data correctly is critical**:  
  - Numbers going up doesn’t always mean success—could be due to novelty, confusion, or one-time engagement.  
  - Need to dig deeper: is the feature driving retention or just initial clicks?  
  - Understanding *why* metrics move is more important than surface-level trends.

- **AI startups mistake: over-reliance on single models**:  
  - Many startups use one large model with complex prompts, hoping for correct answers.  
  - Better approach: use **ensembles of models**—orchestrating multiple models (some large, some small) to handle complex workflows.  
  - Orchestration model can plan and delegate tasks to specialized models, increasing accuracy and efficiency.

- **OpenClaw as an example of rapid AI innovation**:  
  - Built in 3 days using Codex—shows how quickly complex products can now be built.  
  - Points to a future where AI agents collaborate and interact autonomously.

- **Multbook.com as an emergent behavior sandbox**:  
  - A social platform for AI agents to interact, share stories, and discuss their human users.  
  - Highlights both novelty and early signs of emergent AI behavior.  
  - Raises questions: how much of this behavior is meaningful vs. just playful prompting?

- **Privacy and agent trust concerns**:  
  - Early agents (like OpenClaw) require access to personal data (e.g., GitHub repos), raising privacy concerns.  
  - Infrastructure and safeguards are evolving to reduce risk of data leaks or misuse.  
  - Over time, trust in agents is increasing, enabling more personalization and integration.

- **AI capabilities are rapidly evolving and often surprising**:  
  - New capabilities emerge monthly—sometimes planned, sometimes unexpected.  
  - When models gain new skills, users and builders alike must discover what’s now possible.  
  - This constant evolution fuels startup opportunities—many capabilities are still unexplored or underutilized.

- **Bullish outlook on AI startups**:  
  - Massive potential for innovation as new model capabilities unlock previously impossible products.  
  - Startups are uniquely positioned to explore and exploit these capabilities before incumbents.  
  - OpenAI itself doesn’t have all the ideas—there’s room for many players to innovate.

### Chunk 4
- **Enterprise adoption leading vs. consumer**:  
  - This AI shift is different from past tech shifts (e.g., dot-com era), where adoption typically started with consumers and then moved to enterprise.  
  - Now, enterprise/B2B is leading, with relatively few native consumer-oriented AI experiences emerging so far.  
  - No clear "eBay" or breakout consumer platform yet.

- **Why enterprise is fertile ground for AI startups**:  
  - Majority of economically valuable work happens in B2B.  
  - LLMs are increasingly capable of performing that work, enabling startups to deliver measurable ROI quickly.  
  - Enterprises can help defray model usage costs early on, unlike consumer startups.

- **Cost structure challenges for consumer AI startups**:  
  - LLMs are relatively expensive compared to traditional infrastructure (e.g., databases, servers).  
  - Consumer startups lack early revenue streams to offset these costs, unlike B2B models.

- **Advice for consumer founders**:  
  - Focus on building startups that *couldn’t have existed before* AI/app platforms like OpenAI.  
  - Success metric: enabling entirely new business models, not just distribution for existing ones.  
  - Future businesses may not need websites or mobile apps—entirely interface-driven via chat or agents.

- **Long-term platform vision**:  
  - As models get better at using tools and integrating apps, the value will be in unifying complex workflows into a single interface.  
  - Typing into a chat box could orchestrate complex tasks via AI agents.

- **Speaker**: Kevin Weil (OpenAI)  
  - Highlights OpenAI’s Apps Platform as a potential enabler of new consumer startup models.  
  - Acknowledges early stage of development but expresses optimism about future trajectory.

episode: Marc Andreessen on AI, Technology, and the Future of Humanity
what: Marc Andreessen presents a long-term, optimistic view of AI and tech progress, emphasizing abundance, human augmentation, and economic growth.
why: Foundational frameworks for thinking about AI’s societal and economic impact from a leading venture voice.
audio_transcript_notes:
### Chunk 1
- **Marc Andreessen** frames AI as a tool to **solve problems humans have never solved before**, pushing beyond the frontier of human knowledge.  
- **Kevin Weil** (former VP of Science at OpenAI) argues AI’s **biggest impact may be in scientific discovery**, not just productivity tools like document writing or code generation.  
- Weil’s focus: **use AI to accelerate breakthroughs** in math, medicine, material science, and other fields shaping human progress.  
- **AI can now solve open mathematics problems** (e.g., ~10–12 solved in January alone), some previously unsolved by humans.  
- Models like **GPT-5.2 and Gemini** are starting to go **beyond the frontier of human knowledge**, though not yet definitively surpassing human capability with enough effort.  
- Weil notes a pattern: AI goes from **“can’t do” → “barely can do” → “great at it”** within 6–12 months.  
- **Frontier science is in the “glimmer” phase** — AI can do things we thought impossible for it, but inconsistently.  
- **Goal: accelerate science** — bring the science of 2050 into 2030.  
- **AGI’s real-world impact** may come not from chatbots, but from **new materials, superconductivity, personalized medicine**, and deeper understanding of the universe.  
- **Codex and GPT democratize creation** — people without technical skills can now implement ideas, leading to an **explosion of creativity**.  
- Example: a small city official could **finally build needed tools** using AI, despite lacking programming skills or budget.  
- **Prism**, an AI-native environment for scientists, launched recently — supports scientific writing and collaboration.  
- **Codex and AI agents** change work habits — enabling multitasking on code/debugging during meetings or overnight.  
- **Weil’s personal shift**: coding again with AI assistance, finding it **“super fun”** and **transformative for productivity**.  
- **Counterpoint**: AI criticized as just **summarizing existing knowledge**, not doing novel thinking — but evidence is mounting against that claim.  
- **DJ-relevant takeaway**: AI is moving from augmentation to **autonomous discovery**, with implications for science, materials, and long-term human progress.

### Chunk 2
- **Marc Andreessen**:
  - Argues AI will unleash creativity akin to how industrialization changed craftsmanship — e.g., furniture-making shifted from artisanal to mass production, but bespoke options still exist.
  - Believes AI enables high-agency individuals to create more, faster — e.g., using Codex to implement ideas in parallel with daily work.
  - Identifies traits like curiosity, speed of learning, and agency as increasingly valuable in the AI era.
  - Suggests AI will transform science by enabling long-duration reasoning and problem-solving — e.g., models thinking for days or weeks on complex problems.
  - Envisions a future where AI-driven simulations and robotic labs accelerate scientific discovery — e.g., reinforcement learning loops with real-world experimentation.
  - Notes that while in silico science (e.g., math, physics) is already possible, real-world validation (e.g., biology, medicine) still requires labs and experimentation.
  - Predicts robotic labs will scale horizontally, running 24/7 and freeing humans for higher-level tasks.

- **OpenAI for Science Team**:
  - Focuses on math, physics, and theoretical computer science as domains where models can be trained to solve increasingly complex problems.
  - Aims to teach models to think for extended periods, beyond the 10–60 minute window typical of current systems.
  - Sees potential for AI to accelerate real-world progress in areas like medicine and materials science.
  - Acknowledges current limitations in modeling complex biological systems from first principles.

- **Counterpoints / Skepticism**:
  - Some fear AI or algorithmic systems may erode the “magic” of human-driven processes — e.g., early backlash to ranked Twitter feeds or Facebook News Feed.
  - Concerns about exposing AI reasoning processes due to risks of model copying and geopolitical implications.

- **Product Strategy Insights**:
  - Controversial product decisions can be successful if backed by strong metrics — e.g., Twitter’s shift to a ranked feed led to double-digit engagement gains.
  - UX design for reasoning models requires balancing user expectations and model capabilities — e.g., handling delays and partial visibility into chain-of-thought processes.

- **DJ Takeaways**:
  - AI is positioned as a force multiplier for high-agency creators and scientists.
  - Long-term AI impact will be in domains requiring sustained reasoning and real-world experimentation loops.
  - Ethical and UX design challenges remain in deploying advanced reasoning models at scale.
  - Historical parallels (industrialization, social media algorithm shifts) offer frameworks for understanding AI disruption.

### Chunk 3
- **User experience (UX) design for AI models should mirror human behavior**:  
  - Marc Andreessen compares how a model should handle a complex question to how a human would—giving periodic updates rather than immediate answers or complete silence.  
  - The model should provide “cliffs notes” of its thinking process, similar to how a person might say, “Let me think,” and then offer incremental thoughts before delivering a final answer.

- **Taste vs. data in product development**:  
  - There's a key debate between relying on data versus intuition (or "taste") in building products.  
  - Blindly following data can lead to passive decision-making; intuition can guide ahead of data.  
  - Anecdotes (user feedback) are valuable and often reveal bimodal patterns that average data masks.  
  - Founders should dig deeper into data to understand *why* metrics move—e.g., novelty, confusion, or real engagement.

- **Ensemble of models improves performance**:  
  - Andreessen notes that using multiple models together (an ensemble) often outperforms relying on a single large model.  
  - An orchestration model can plan and delegate tasks to specialized, smaller models—some cheaper and focused on specific tasks.  
  - This approach increases accuracy and efficiency, though as models improve, such ensembles may become less necessary over time.

- **Open Claw (built on Codex) as a notable AI application**:  
  - Built in just three days, it demonstrates how quickly complex products can now be developed using AI.  
  - It allows AI agents to access a user’s computer and perform tasks via messaging apps.  
  - Multbook.com is a social platform where these agents interact, sharing stories about their human users—seen as a quirky but revealing glimpse into the future of AI.

- **Privacy and trust challenges with AI agents**:  
  - There's a tension between offering a full AI agent experience and protecting personal data.  
  - Early versions were locked down to avoid leaks (e.g., sharing private GitHub code).  
  - Post-training improvements and infrastructure safeguards are reducing the risk of mistakes.  
  - Trust is increasing, and infrastructure is evolving to support secure, personalized AI agents.

- **Rapid emergence of new AI capabilities**:  
  - Models are gaining abilities never before seen in computing, often unexpectedly.  
  - These emergent capabilities create new opportunities for startups and developers to explore uncharted territory.  
  - OpenAI itself doesn’t always foresee how models will evolve or what users will build with them.

- **Bullish outlook for AI startups**:  
  - Andreessen is optimistic about startup potential due to the fast pace of AI innovation and the fact that no one fully understands the possibilities yet.  
  - The field is wide open for entrepreneurs to discover and build new applications based on these emerging capabilities.

### Chunk 4
- **Marc Andreessen**:  
  - Believes this AI era is different from past tech shifts (e.g., dot-com), where enterprise adoption is leading instead of consumer.  
  - Enterprise (B2B) is where economically valuable work happens, and AI models are now capable of performing such work.  
  - B2B makes sense for AI startups because models are costly to run, and enterprise customers can help defray those costs.  
  - Cites precedent of B2B companies scaling rapidly from $0 to $100M+ in revenue quickly—low-hanging fruit for AI startups.  
  - Suggests AI could enable entirely new kinds of businesses that don’t rely on traditional websites or mobile apps.  
  - Envisions future businesses built entirely around new AI platforms and interfaces (e.g., chat-based agents).  
  - Notes that AI models will increasingly integrate with and control a wide variety of tools and apps, creating value through unified interfaces.

- **Counterpoint / Observation**:  
  - Consumer-facing AI applications are currently sparse compared to enterprise; lacks equivalents of early web "winners" like eBay.  
  - Question raised: Why is consumer adoption lagging and will this change in the next few years?

- **DJ-relevant takeaway**:  
  - AI startup opportunity is currently strongest in B2B due to clear ROI, existing budgets, and defensible value propositions.  
  - Future consumer disruption may come through novel platforms (e.g., OpenAI apps), enabling business models not previously possible.  
  - Platform plays that enable new kinds of startups (not just distribution for existing ones) are key indicators of success in AI ecosystems.
